question: Electrolux restructuring in Italy: closure of the Cerreto d’Esi plant and 1 700 redundancies

On 11 May 2026, the Swedish group Electrolux announced a restructuring plan that provides for some 1 700 redundancies of 4 500 employees in Italy and the definitive closure of the Cerreto d’Esi (Ancona) plant, which employs 170 people. The plan involves all the group’s Italian production sites: Porcia, Susegana, Forlì and Solaro.

The trade unions Fim, Fiom and Uilm declared the plan ‘unacceptable’ and announced an open-ended period of industrial action. The workers caught up in the plans will be difficult to relocate in the short term, causing serious economic and social repercussions for the regions in question. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the conditions have been met for the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund to be mobilised to provide support for those workers and their families?

How will it ensure that Electrolux complies with the obligations laid down in Directive 2002/14/EC and Directive 98/59/EC on collective redundancies that workers must be informed and consulted in advance?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF) is directed at supporting active labour market policy measures and personalised services that aim to support workers’ job transitions, helping them to reintegrate into decent and sustainable employment.

Support through the EGF may be deployed for dismissed workers if the Member State applies and the criteria defined in the Regulation1 are fulfilled. Companies planning to dismiss 200 or more workers can now request EGF co-financing to support these workers through the EGF Managing Authority2 in the EU country where the layoffs will take place, enabling early intervention before dismissals occur.

Such requests must be submitted within 14 weeks of notifying workers' representatives about the redundancies. The Commission has no powers to intervene in specific company decisions such as those at issue. However, companies have to respect the body of EU law, which includes directives on information and consultation of employees3 and on collective redundancies4.

They lay down minimum requirements for the protection of workers by providing for information and consultation of workers’ representatives on matters affecting workers’ jobs, and when envisaging collective redundancies. Member States must transpose and implement EU Directives, and Italy has transposed both Directives into national law5.

It is for the competent national authorities, including the courts, to ensure that an individual employer complies with the relevant national rules transposing the Directives, having regard to the specific circumstances of each case.

4 Council Directive 98/59/EC of 20 July 1998 on the approximation of the laws of the Member States relating to collective redundancies, OJ L 225, 12.8.1998, p. 16–21 - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1998/59/oj/eng. 5 by Legislative Decree of 6 February 2007, No 25; and by the law of 23 July 1991, n. 223, as further amended.
